newsitem.title: CHINA: China to play host to rare debate on human rights.
newsitem.headline: China to play host to rare debate on human rights.

text.p: Members of parliament from around the world will bring a rare open debate on human rights to China next week during an international parliamentary meeting, conference officials said on Friday.

Beijing's sensitivity to criticism of its human rights record would not stand in the way of a general debate on rights issues at the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) conference that opens in Beijing on Monday, the officials said.

Around 600 members of parliament would gather in Beijing for five days to discuss human rights, food issues and other matters of international concern, Dr Ahmed Fathy Sorour, president of the international network of legislators, told a news conference.

"We will have a general discussion on the general promotion and respect of human rights which is an item of the conference and will be discussed by committee in public," said IPU Secretary-General Pierre Cornillon.
China rejects most foreign criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs and routinely refuses visas to rights groups it considers hostile.
The parliamentary conference will be the first time China has permitted open debate on human rights by foreigners since the U.N. World Conference on Women in Beijing last year.

Officials of the biannual parliamentary conference said the rights debate would be an open platform for the views of delegates from the more than 100 parliaments taking part, but would not be followed by a resolution or vote.
"MPs (members of parliament) can get up and say anything they want at all," said IPU information officer Robin Newmann.

China, represented by members of its largely rubber-stamp National People's Congress, had invited the IPU to hold the conference in Beijing two years ago, while the union had only chosen to debate human rights last year, officials said.

Rights group Amnesty International, long condemned by Beijing for its reports of widespread abuses in Chinese prisons and elsewhere, was attending as an observer and would submit a statement to the meeting, an Amnesty official said.
The statement would refer to the plan of action adopted at last year's Women's Conference, said the official, who declined to be identified.

"We are basically calling on parliamentarians to do whatever they can to persuade their governments to put these commitments into action," the official said, but gave no details of whether the group would specifically raise China's rights record.

Apart from human rights and food issues, the conference will also choose a supplementary item for discussion from proposals ranging from a ban on anti-personnel mines to U.S. laws aimed at cutting foreign investment in Cuba, Iran and Libya.

An emergency proposal from Baghdad for the parlimentarians to debate recent U.S. attacks on Iraq would also be considered but would need approval from 80 percent of the members to be permitted, officials said.
U.S. members of Congress would not be present to discuss their nation's conduct because of the imminent presidential and congressional elections, they said.
U.S. Congress members have attended IPU meetings since 1938 but have been less active since the 1980s, with some calling for the United States to leave the organisation altogether.
